processes.description: Rounds start when the California ISO, FERC or a regulatory colleague issues a notice, order, draft market design or procedure update, often forwarded to the real-time desk by its lead. The lead sums up what changes (price caps, underscheduling penalties, ancillary service and grid management charges, refunds), asks colleagues for views or a meeting, and puts implementation questions to the ISO. Some rounds ask for comments on drafts by a same-day deadline or set up testing against new schemas, test servers and market simulations.
steps: The ISO, FERC or a regulatory colleague circulates a notice, order, proposal or operating procedure update.
The desk lead forwards it with a short note on what it means or a question for the team.
The team reads the order or posted documents and works out the effect on scheduling, price caps, penalties and charges.
Where comments are invited, drafts are reviewed and comments go to the named contacts by the stated deadline.
Implementation questions go back to the ISO, and test servers or market simulation sessions are arranged for system changes.
The team meets or replies on how its practice changes, such as outage notification or tagging.

stalls.summary: The automation specifications the ISO posted had problems in their pdf versions, so documents needed for system changes had to be reissued or worked around.
Changes reach the desk close to go-live, so questions on how a new pricing mechanism or security upgrade will work, and requests for a test server, are raised just before implementation.

contradictions.summary: The ISO's market design proposal sets goals for the real-time market that the desk lead reads as at odds with each other.
A FERC order on refunds departs from the commission's own earlier holdings in the same proceeding without explaining why.
On the same day the price cap is described both as a retroactive cap during mitigation hours and as an unrevised cap needing confirmation from the ISO, leaving the applicable cap unclear.

automation.approach: A shared regulatory change log fed by ISO and FERC notices, each entry tagged by topic (price caps, penalties, charges, schemas, operating procedures) with an owner, effective date, comment deadline and the agreed scheduling impact, plus an impact checklist the desk works through for each change: systems, settlements, tagging, outage notice, testing.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are notices forwarded with a question about what they mean for the desk; the same impact questions recur (caps, penalties, charges, system interfaces, testing). A checklist makes each review cover them consistently and leaves a record, while reading the rule and judging its effect stays with the traders and schedulers.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is reading the order, notice or posted documents behind each email and working out what changes for scheduling and settlements: price caps, penalties, charges, schemas. A routine procedure update takes about 10 minutes; a FERC order or draft market design that needs a desk view or comments by a deadline takes about 60, and system changes add test-server or simulation set-up. A tagged change log and impact checklist would take over sorting and tracking; interpreting the rule stays with people.

processes.description: A round starts when an organiser, often an assistant or a group lead, announces a staff, group or customer meeting, conference call or lunch, asks people to hold or clear a date, or asks which day suits. Replies confirm attendance or offer alternatives, someone reserves a conference room and finalises numbers for catering, and now and then the meeting is cancelled or moved and a fresh notice goes out.
steps: An organiser proposes a meeting, call, lunch or off-site and asks attendees to hold a date or say whether it suits.
Attendees reply with their availability or attendance.
The organiser reserves a conference room and confirms the time and place.
Numbers are finalised for lunch or catering where food is involved.
If plans change, the meeting is cancelled or moved and a new notice goes out.

stalls.summary: Headcounts for lunches and off-sites wait on attendance replies before numbers can be finalised.
Meetings already arranged are sometimes cancelled, so arrangements are undone and the meeting has to be set up again in another form.

automation.approach: Shared calendar invitations with room booking and built-in RSVP tracking, so the organiser sends one invitation, sees replies tallied for catering, and reissues one updated invitation when a meeting moves or is cancelled; a standard meeting notice carries date, time, room and the reply deadline.
automation.rationale: The rounds are short notices and attendance requests that repeat the same fields: date, time, room, purpose, reply needed by. A reusable notice keeps them complete and makes replies easy to tally; choosing the date and handling cancellations stay with the organiser.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work outside the emails is checking calendars for a suitable date, reserving a room, and for lunches or off-sites totalling attendance and arranging catering. A regular meeting in a standing room takes a few minutes; an off-site lunch with headcount and catering takes nearer 20. A shared calendar with room booking and RSVP tallying covers about half of it; picking dates and handling cancellations stay with people.

processes.description: Rounds start when a contract administrator, volume analyst or field contact finds a meter's gas not allocating correctly, or a deal or contract change means a meter must move to another contract for given months. The request names the meter, the months and the target contract; someone in logistics or volume management changes the allocation set-up, reviews the attached allocation statements, and checks that volumes have been actualised. Some changes are wanted urgently for economics, and some wait on legal or another party first.
steps: Someone spots a meter whose volumes are not allocating correctly, or a deal change that needs a different allocation.
A request names the meter, the production months and the contract the volumes should go to.
The allocation set-up is changed: contract, ranking, percentages or volume overrides.
Allocation statements are reviewed and corrections agreed with the responsible scheduler.
Volumes are checked in Volume Management once actualised, and the corrected allocation is confirmed.
Questions needing other teams, such as legal, are referred and the change waits for their answer.

stalls.summary: The person handed an allocation change understood it differently from the requester, so an urgent change had to be redone.
A correction waited on a call back from a counterpart who first had to speak with Legal.
With volumes not yet actualised and nothing showing in Volume Management, nobody was sure who had to talk to whom to get the allocation fixed.
Meters already known not to allocate properly still turned up with gas allocating incorrectly, so the same fault came round again.

automation.approach: An exception report comparing each meter's allocated volumes with its contract, ranking and percentage set-up, flagging meters that fail to allocate or land on the wrong contract, paired with a standard change request form naming the meter, months, target contract, ranking or percentage, requester and the owner in volume management who makes the change.
automation.rationale: The stalls come from requests understood differently, unclear owners and changes waiting on others. A request form with fixed fields and a named owner removes most of the handoff confusion, and the exception report finds faults before counterparts do; deciding which contract is right stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is tracing why a meter's volumes land on the wrong contract, changing the allocation set-up for each affected month, rerunning and reviewing the allocation statement, and checking Volume Management once volumes are actualised. Moving one meter to a named contract takes about 15 minutes; several months of rework or a fault that needs investigation runs to 90. An exception report and prefilled change form would take over finding and recording faults; choosing the right contract stays with people.
